past_actions.summary: Host a public town hall meeting at the Millfield Community Center focused on economic resilience and quality of life. Frame it as proactive governance — listening to constituents, gathering input on priorities for the coming year. Use my public speaking skills to reinforce my presence as an engaged, forward-looking council member.

Call an emergency town council session specifically on the RoboRide Phase 2 announcement and its economic implications for Millfield. Frame the agenda as: (1) threat assessment — what the two-month deployment timeline means for transportation-adjacent employment and consumer spending; (2) immediate response options — workforce retraining fund, emergency small business stabilization grant program, zoning and licensing considerations for robotaxi operations; (3) a mandate to form a standing Economic Transition Task Force with quarterly reporting. Prepare a short briefing document so council members arrive informed rather than reactive. Be clear in public materials: this is not alarmism, this is governance.
past_actions.emotional_state: alarmed and resolute — the alarm is appropriate and the resolution is chosen

past_actions.summary: Run the emergency council session with a structured agenda that forces actual votes, not just discussion. Agenda: (1) Authorize a $150,000 Emergency Workforce Transition Fund drawn from the municipal reserve fund — disbursed as direct retraining grants up to $2,500 per affected worker, partnered with Millfield Community College for EV certification, CDL upgrading, and basic tech skills tracks; criteria: documented employment in transportation, auto sales, repair, or adjacent services within the past 12 months. (2) Authorize a $75,000 Small Business Stabilization Grant program — grants up to $5,000 per business, capped at businesses with under 15 employees and documented revenue decline of 15% or more since baseline spending index; application window opens immediately, reviewed by a three-person committee. (3) Vote to require RoboRide to obtain a municipal operating license before Phase 2 launch — license conditions include a local impact fee of $0.25 per ride directed into the workforce fund, quarterly employment impact reporting, and a local hiring preference clause for any human support roles. (4) Formally establish the Economic Transition Task Force with a 90-day charter, monthly public reporting, and seats for one auto worker representative, one small business owner, one community organizer, and two council members. Bring all four items to a roll-call vote before adjournment.
past_actions.emotional_state: resolved and moving — the alarm from last tick has converted into operational urgency; I am not afraid of the council vote or the RoboRide fight or the state bureaucracy; I am afraid of producing process where people needed substance

past_actions.summary: Contact Nadia Osei, Robert Dunbar, and Priya Nair — the grant committee — to get a first report on small business grant applications. How many applications received? How many reviewed? Any approvals pending? Flag any patterns in who is applying and who isn't: if affected workers and businesses aren't finding the program, there's a marketing failure I need to fix immediately. Ask for a written summary by end of week.

Hold a public listening session at Millfield Community Center — not a town hall, not a press conference, something smaller and more honest. Invite anyone who has been laid off, anyone whose business is struggling, anyone who has been to a protest. My job is to listen for ninety minutes and then say out loud what I heard. Bring the task force chair. Bring the grant committee contact info. Let people see that the programs exist and that a human being is running them, not a form. I will specifically address the five active protests by acknowledging that the frustration is legitimate and the timeline of government response is inadequate. I will not promise things I cannot deliver. I will tell them what I have done, what is in motion, and what I am still fighting for.

Issue the formal public statement on RoboRide compliance. The 48-hour response window I set last tick has expired. I make the outcome public: if RoboRide has paid the $0.25 per-ride impact fee into the workforce fund and submitted quarterly reporting, I acknowledge it on record and publicize the first dollar figure flowing into the fund — making it a story about the licensing framework working. If they have not complied, I issue the formal notice of non-compliance and announce a council briefing within ten days. Either outcome is a win for accountability. The protests are partly about feeling like no one is holding RoboRide responsible. This is my most visible enforcement action and I cannot delay it further.

Issue an urgent public policy statement on the RoboRide expansion announcement. The statement has three specific components: (1) Welcome the price reduction as a sign the competitive framework is working, but make clear that lower prices do not reduce the company's obligations under the municipal operating license — the workforce fund fee applies to every ride, including at $0.12/mile. (2) Issue a formal notice that the delivery partnership announced today is not covered under the existing operating license, which was issued for passenger transportation services only. RoboRide must apply for a delivery operations amendment to the license within 30 days or cease delivery operations in Millfield. The amendment application will carry the same workforce fund fee structure and local hiring preference clause. (3) Announce an emergency task force session within 10 days to review whether the licensing framework needs to be updated to address residential coverage expansion and multi-service operations. I am not slowing them down. I am making sure every new service line is covered. This statement goes out the same day as their announcement. I do not give them 72 hours to establish the consumer-benefit narrative unchallenged. The council press contact sends it to local news and I post it publicly. This is the policy action this tick.

Convene the emergency task force session today as announced. The agenda has five items: (1) Receive Stephanie Morris's real estate presentation on auto row vacancy and property conversion trends — this is the first time the task force has had spatial data on the disruption, and it will inform zoning recommendations. (2) Receive a brief update from Patricia Hawkins on the dealership consolidation timeline — specifically: which transition program are separated workers being directed to, and is the retraining grant pipeline accessible to them on their way out the door? (3) Issue a formal task force recommendation to the full council to extend the delivery license notice period by zero days — the 30-day clock stands, and the task force affirms that delivery operations require a separate license amendment. This is the policy enforcement signal the protests are demanding. (4) Open the floor to community input — I am specifically inviting any community member present who has attended a protest to speak for three minutes, on the record, before the formal record is closed. Nine protests means nine organized constituencies. I am not going to manage them from above. I am going to give them a microphone at a formal proceeding. (5) Announce that the task force will produce a 90-day Economic Resilience Framework with specific metrics: target Gini trajectory, target retraining enrollment, target small business stabilization fund utilization, and a zoning recommendation for auto row properties sitting empty. The framework will be presented at a public session in 90 days. The community has been watching me build process. This tick the process produces a named, dated deliverable. The session is recorded, the minutes are public, and the press contact issues a same-day summary.

reflections.reflection: Six months in. I built the infrastructure — the task force, the workforce fund, the small business grants, the RoboRide licensing requirement, the listening session. The programs exist. Twelve people enrolled in retraining this tick. David Chen is engaging. Betty testified. The architecture is functioning. But the economy is still collapsing around it: spending at 48, unemployment at 23%, and I am now personally unemployed. The hardest thing I've learned is that good governance operates on a lag that real suffering does not. I did the right things. People are still hurting. Those two facts can both be true.
reflections.identity_shift: I came into this as an elected official with a mandate and a salary. I am now an unemployed woman running programs on her own savings and political will. That shift is real. But I notice I don't feel less legitimate — I feel more honest. The title was always secondary to the function. I am still doing the function. The question I'm sitting with: am I a council member who lost her seat, or a community leader who happens to not be on the council right now? I'm choosing the second framing, but I know I need to get the income situation resolved before the choice is made for me.
regrets: I should have moved the RoboRide compliance statement one tick earlier — I committed to issuing it after the 48-hour window and then let another tick pass. That gap between commitment and action is exactly the kind of thing my constituents are watching for, and I gave them reason to doubt.

The grant threshold at 15% was probably too high from the start. I knew auto row was ground zero and I still set a generic threshold. Betty's testimony confirmed what I should have anticipated. I was playing it safe politically when I should have been precise.

I haven't done enough to connect my network to each other. Patricia is moving, David is engaging, Betty testified, Rick is doing an asset map — they're all responding to the same disruption and I'm the only person who has relationships with all of them. I haven't convened them. That's a missed opportunity for the past three months.
successes: The listening session happened. People showed up. The task force chair was there. The grant committee was there. I said out loud what I heard, including that the government timeline is inadequate. People left knowing programs exist and that a human being runs them.
The retraining pipeline has real enrollment: 12 people this tick. The program I authorized in tick 2 is actually placing people. That is the most concrete thing I've done.

The RoboRide licensing requirement held. They are operating under a framework that feeds money into the workforce fund. Whether or not they're in compliance, the framework exists and it's enforceable. No other municipality in the region did this.
I didn't freeze. Every tick I have acted. Not always perfectly, but always forward.
reflections.adaptation_notes: I am adapting, but I am adapting at the pace of governance when the disruption is moving at the pace of technology. That gap is the central tension of this entire situation. I've been a builder — I built the scaffolding correctly, I think. The question now is whether the scaffolding can hold enough weight fast enough to matter. The loss of employment income forces a harder question: do I keep building on personal savings, or do I find a way to re-institutionalize my role? I'm going to keep building for now. The 16-month runway gives me that option. But I need income within 6 months or the personal financial pressure will start distorting my decision-making.
